turns.prompt_text: Of these three weed wackers which one should I buy? They are each $10 at rummage, rampage and Ames Attached 1 file. - 4d4ca5c9-f531-484e-8d6f-efe5da6449e5
turns.response_html:
The Clear Winner: Echo GT-225

You should definitely grab the orange Echo GT-225 on the far left. At $10, it is an absolute steal compared to the other two options.

Here is the breakdown of why the Echo is the best choice:

  • Build Quality: Echo is a highly reputable, prosumer-grade brand known for outstanding durability and reliable engines. The two green trimmers are Weed Eater FeatherLites (the FL 21 and XT 260), which are budget, entry-level consumer models that are notoriously finicky and often treated as disposable once they stop running.
  • Repairability: Buying a $10 gas trimmer at a rummage sale usually means it might need a little TLC to get running perfectly. Parts for the Echo are cheap and readily available. If it just needs a quick carburetor clean or a new fuel line, it will be a straightforward mechanical project to tackle out in your dad's workshop.
  • Ergonomics: The GT-225 is a curved-shaft trimmer, which can sometimes deflect debris a bit awkwardly depending on your swing. You can easily loosen the screws on the black D-handle and rotate it to get a much more comfortable left-handed grip.

Grab the Echo, pick up some fresh 50:1 premix fuel, and you'll have a fantastic machine.

turns.prompt_text: So what kind of fuels primers and strings do I need? I'm at Walmart so I imagine I might be able to pick them up
turns.response_html:
Since you are already at Walmart, you should be able to find everything you need in the lawn and garden section to get that Echo running perfectly:

Fuel (50:1 Ratio) The Echo GT-225 requires a 50:1 gas-to-oil mix. You have two options here: you can buy a small bottle of 50:1 2-cycle engine oil to mix with a gallon of fresh mid-grade or premium gas, or you can grab a can of pre-mixed 50:1 fuel (like TruFuel) right off the shelf for immediate use.

String (.095-inch) You will need .095-inch diameter trimmer line. The GT-225 features a "rapid-loader" head that uses individual 8-inch strips of line rather than winding a continuous spool. You can buy a standard bulk spool of .095 line and simply cut your own 8-inch lengths to save a lot of money over time compared to buying the pre-cut packs.

Primer Bulb If the old one is cracked or missing, the GT-225 uses a standard Zama/Walbro style purge bulb (Echo part P005003120). Walmart usually sells universal 2-cycle primer bulb replacement kits (often from brands like Arnold). These blister packs come with a few different sizes, and the standard 3/4-inch base bulb included in the pack will pop right into your carburetor.

turns.prompt_text: It looks like I'm missing the head Also, do I need the fuel and a primer separately Attached 1 file. - 8d70ecbc-dec6-412e-be62-5edb54147453
turns.response_html:
Good news—you aren't actually missing the head!

The black circular part in your photo is the complete Echo Rapid-Loader trimmer head. The orange bits stuck in the center are just the remnants of the old trimmer line. To load it, you simply pull those old orange pieces out (you might need pliers if they are jammed) and slide new 8-inch strips of .095 line through the eyelets. The head has an internal cam that grabs the line and holds it tight.

Regarding the fuel and primer, yes, they are two completely different things:

  • Fuel is the liquid 50:1 gas-and-oil mixture that goes into the gas tank to run the engine. You will absolutely need this.
  • Primer (Primer Bulb) is a small, clear rubber button located on the side of the engine's carburetor. You press it a few times before starting the machine to pull fuel from the tank into the carburetor.

What you need to buy right now: You definitely need to buy the 50:1 fuel and the .095 trimmer line. You only need to buy a primer bulb kit if the little clear rubber bubble currently on the machine is cracked, brittle, or completely missing. If the rubber bulb is intact and squishes normally when you press it, skip buying a replacement for now.

turns.response_html:
Yes, you have great options right there on the shelf for your 50:1 Echo!

1. Ready-to-Use Pre-Mixed Fuel (Easiest)

  • Bottom shelf, center-right: Grab the red metal can labeled 50:1 MIX ENGINEERED FUEL + OIL (priced at $7.74 on the shelf tag).
  • Why: It’s ethanol-free, pre-mixed to the exact ratio your Echo needs, and ready to pour straight into the gas tank with zero effort.

2. Mix-Your-Own Oil (Cheapest Long-Term)

  • Top shelf, left side: Pick up a bottle of the Super Tech 2-Cycle Engine Oil (the small blue bottles, $1.58–$1.68).
  • Why: You pour one small bottle into 1 gallon of fresh gas from a gas station pump to make your own 50:1 mix.

💡 Extra Tip

If you ended up needing a primer bulb after all, look right at the top shelf tag labeled UNIV PRIMER BULBS ($8.96)—the replacement kit should be hanging on the peg hooks right above those oil bottles.

Avoid:

  • The green can on the bottom shelf (40:1 mix - wrong ratio).
  • The bright red bottles on the upper right (4-Cycle oil - will ruin a 2-stroke engine).
  • The big blue bottle on the far right (Bar & Chain Oil - meant for chainsaws).

turns.prompt_text: What does semi-synthetic or full synthetic mean and how much does it matter?
turns.response_html:
Here is the breakdown of what those terms mean in the world of 2-cycle engine oil and how much it actually matters for your machine:

The Basics

In a 2-cycle engine like your Echo, the oil is mixed directly with the gas. This means the oil has to lubricate the internal moving parts and then successfully burn off in the combustion chamber.

  • Semi-Synthetic: This is a blend of traditional mineral oil (refined from crude oil) and artificially engineered synthetic oils. It offers a good middle-ground: it lubricates better and burns cleaner than old-school standard oil, but keeps the price low.
  • Full Synthetic: This is chemically engineered in a lab from the ground up. The molecules are uniform in size, which means it provides superior lubrication at high temperatures. Most importantly, it burns extremely clean.

How Much Does It Matter?

For a 2-cycle weed wacker, it matters when it comes to carbon buildup.

Because the engine is actively burning the oil along with the gas, standard and semi-synthetic oils tend to leave behind a bit of soot (carbon) inside the engine. Over time, this carbon can clog the spark arrestor screen on the muffler, gunk up the piston, and make the trimmer run rough or refuse to start. Full synthetic oil burns almost completely away, leaving very little residue behind and producing noticeably less smoke while you work.

The Verdict for Your Echo: Since you are mixing such small batches (one tiny bottle to a whole gallon of gas), the cost difference between semi-synthetic and full synthetic is literally pennies per tank.

If they have a Full Synthetic option on the shelf (often in gray or silver bottles, or clearly labeled on the Super Tech options), grab that one. It will keep your $10 Echo running cleaner and significantly reduce the chances of you needing to tear apart the engine to clean out carbon deposits later. If they only have Semi-Synthetic in the 50:1 blue bottles, it is still perfectly fine to use and won't harm the engine at all.

turns.prompt_text: What kind of pump fuel can this take? E87 or E88? I assume no ethanol
turns.response_html:
You are right to be cautious about ethanol, as it is the number one enemy of small 2-cycle engines.

Here is exactly what you need to look for at the gas pump:

  • Octane Rating: Echo requires a minimum of 89 octane (mid-grade) or higher. Do not use standard 87 octane (regular), as it can cause the high-revving engine to run too hot or knock.
  • Ethanol Content: You want 0% ethanol (ethanol-free) if possible. If you cannot find a pump with ethanol-free gas, standard pump gas with up to 10% ethanol (E10) is acceptable, but you should not let it sit in the machine for more than 30 days without a fuel stabilizer.

Stay away from E88 (Unleaded 88) When you see "88" at the pump (often labeled as Unleaded 88 or E15), it typically means the fuel contains 15% ethanol. Never put this in your weed wacker. Any fuel with more than 10% ethanol (like E15 or E85) will run too hot, melt fuel lines, and permanently destroy small engines.

To play it safe and keep things simple, go to the pump and select the Premium (91 or 93 octane) or Mid-grade (89 octane) button, and make sure there are no warning stickers saying it contains more than 10% ethanol!

turns.prompt_text: I don't currently have a gas can to put it in. Can I just put it in like a milk? Jug or does the plastic really matter?
turns.response_html:
Absolutely do not use a milk jug. The type of plastic matters immensely.

Here is why you need a proper gas can:

  • Chemical Breakdown: Milk jugs are made of thin plastic that is not chemically treated to withstand petroleum products. Gasoline will quickly degrade and dissolve the plastic, leading to a puddle of highly flammable gas in your vehicle or on your garage floor.
  • Expansion and Pressure: Gasoline creates fumes that expand depending on the temperature. A proper gas can is thick enough and vented appropriately to handle this pressure. A milk jug will swell, split, or pop open.
  • It Is Illegal and Unsafe: It is against the law—and against the safety policies of every gas station—to dispense fuel into an unapproved container. Gas stations require fuel to be pumped into designated, color-coded containers (red for gasoline) that meet DOT and EPA safety standards.

Your Best Options Right Now: Since you are still at Walmart, you have two easy solutions:

  1. Buy a 1-Gallon Gas Can: Walk over to the automotive aisle or look around the lawn and garden section. A small, 1-gallon red plastic gas can usually costs less than $10.
  2. Buy the Pre-Mixed Fuel: If you don't want to buy and store a gas can today, grab the metal can of 50:1 Engineered Fuel we looked at earlier. The metal can it comes in is already rated for fuel storage, so you won't need a separate gas can at all.
